Consistency.justification: The proposal is strongly aligned with the core idea of using SCAT to analyze ethics-committee comments concerning non-medical research at a Japanese university. Its attention to actual review concerns, disciplined qualitative coding, and transparent documentation also responds directly to the gaps identified in the related-work discussion. However, several elements weaken internal consistency. Five disciplines crossed with five study types create up to 25 strata, so a quota of 6–10 proposals per stratum is incompatible with the stated total of 40–60 proposals. The title and some claims refer broadly to Japan even though data come from one university. In addition, the extensive privacy, differential privacy, NLP, clustering, and randomized workflow components create scope beyond the central SCAT research question and are not always integrated clearly with the substantive analysis of ethical-review practices.

Clarity.justification: The proposal has a clear central topic, a structured workflow, named comparison conditions, concrete reliability and privacy metrics, and an unusually explicit description of governance procedures. The SCAT stages and intended outputs are understandable. Important details nevertheless remain ambiguous: the unit of analysis for coding is not specified; it is unclear whether reliability is computed at the excerpt, comment, proposal, code, or theme level; the construction and role of the held-out test set are not explained; and the saturation criterion and preregistered re-identification threshold lack numerical definitions. The relationship between SCAT, NLP-generated candidates, and final theorization also needs clarification. The large number of auxiliary components makes the proposal more complex than necessary and obscures which analyses are primary, exploratory, or methodological.

Novelty.justification: The substantive focus on non-medical REC review comments in Japan appears comparatively underexplored, and the combination of a documented SCAT protocol, bilingual codebook, formal intercoder assessment, NLP assistance, and adversarial privacy evaluation is a fresh and potentially useful methodological package. The strongest originality lies in integrating reproducibility and privacy safeguards into a small-corpus qualitative study. However, none of the individual components is fundamentally new: SCAT, double-coding, codebook versioning, embedding-based clustering, k-anonymity, differential privacy, and simulated linkage attacks are established techniques. The proposal therefore offers notable synthesis and application-level novelty rather than a clearly new qualitative, statistical, or machine-learning method.

Soundness.justification: The proposal includes several sound practices, including calibration, double-coding, codebook versioning, back-translation, confidence intervals, ablations, secure data handling, and explicit recognition of limitations. However, major methodological gaps limit rigor. A sample of 40–60 proposals is unlikely to support reliable comparisons across as many as 25 discipline-by-study-type cells, and chi-square assumptions will frequently fail; Fisher's exact tests do not solve the underlying low-power problem. Comments and themes nested within proposals may also violate independence assumptions, but no hierarchical or repeated-measures analysis is proposed. The hypothesis that Krippendorff's alpha will reach at least 0.80 is framed more as a desired threshold than a theoretically motivated empirical prediction, and code prevalence can make both alpha and kappa unstable. Coding units, missing-data handling, multilabel reliability, coder-condition assignment, multiplicity correction, and power analysis are unspecified. Randomly assigning coders to conditions risks confounding coder ability with workflow condition unless the design is crossed or counterbalanced. Reconciliation should be separated from pre-reconciliation reliability measurement. Cluster purity requires defensible reference labels, while topic coherence may not be meaningful for UMAP and HDBSCAN clusters on a very small corpus. Applying k-anonymity to free text does not by itself provide a robust privacy guarantee, embedding nearest-neighbor linkage lacks a calibrated threat model, and differential privacy aggregates do not protect the underlying released text. These issues are reparable but substantial.

Feasibility.justification: Most individual activities are technically possible with current tools, and the proposal appropriately plans for institutional approval, local NLP processing, access controls, staged de-identification, and human oversight. Nonetheless, the complete plan is ambitious for only 40–60 proposals. It requires access to highly sensitive records, bilingual coders, an independent translation reviewer, multiple experimental coding conditions, repeated double-coding, secure infrastructure or an HSM, public-source adversarial testing, several privacy settings, differential privacy analyses, and NLP model evaluation. The stated stratified quotas cannot be met within the target sample size. A 10-proposal held-out set further reduces the material available for calibration, condition comparisons, and subgroup inference. Legal approval may prevent access, while heavy redaction may make SCAT interpretation difficult. Feasibility would improve substantially by reducing the number of strata and experimental conditions, treating NLP and privacy experiments as secondary pilots, and specifying available personnel, timeline, and compute resources.

Significance.justification: Understanding how ethics committees evaluate non-medical research is important because governance frameworks and published evidence often focus more heavily on biomedical research. A transparent typology of concerns could improve committee guidance, applicant training, review consistency, and institutional policy. The bilingual codebook and privacy-aware workflow could also be useful to other Japanese institutions. The likely impact is constrained by the single-university sample, small corpus, uncertain transferability across institutional settings, and the possibility that extensive methodological experimentation will displace deeper interpretation of review practices. The study could make a meaningful domain contribution, but claims about ethical review in Japan as a whole would require multi-institutional replication.

strengths: Directly addresses an underexamined and practically important question about non-medical research ethics review in Japan through a structured SCAT analysis.
Provides unusually strong attention to documentation, bilingual coding, intercoder assessment, data governance, de-identification, and reproducible workflow design.
Explicitly acknowledges legal, privacy, sampling, translation, resource, NLP, and generalizability risks.
weaknesses: The proposed 6–10 cases per discipline-by-study-type stratum is mathematically incompatible with a total sample of 40–60, and subgroup tests would be severely underpowered.

Key statistical and qualitative design details are missing, including coding units, multilabel reliability procedures, power analysis, multiplicity control, nesting, and a counterbalanced coder-condition design.
The privacy and NLP components are overextended for the corpus size, and k-anonymity or differentially private aggregates do not establish that sensitive text can be released safely.
Evidence from one university cannot substantiate broad claims about Japan without careful framing or external replication.
